claims.text: Temperature-dependent lattice distortions preferentially localize at microstructural interfaces in HfNbTaTiZr.
Localized lattice distortions cause spatially inhomogeneous thermal expansion.
Differential thermal expansion at interfaces generates local thermal stresses.
The local thermal stresses change the balance between dislocation glide and climb.
Local thermal stresses alter phase stability in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed interface-stress mechanism governs the alloy's high-temperature creep behavior.
The proposed interface-stress mechanism governs the temperature evolution of elastic modulus.
The proposed interface-stress mechanism contributes to strain hardening during cold rolling.
The proposed interface-stress and phase-stability mechanism contributes to hardening during aging at 600–800 °C.
Conventionally processed, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr has a composite microstructure with grain boundaries and possible incipient segregation.
Grain boundaries and phase interfaces are locations where thermal-expansion mismatch is pronounced.
Homogenizing grain-boundary structure will reduce interface heterogeneity and thermal-expansion mismatch.
Engineering greater interface heterogeneity will accentuate thermal-expansion mismatch.
Samples with enhanced thermal-expansion mismatch will have higher steady-state creep rates at high temperature than homogenized samples.
Samples with enhanced thermal-expansion mismatch will show anomalous elastic-modulus softening or hardening relative to homogenized samples.
Samples with enhanced thermal-expansion mismatch will show distinct microhardness evolution relative to homogenized samples.
Minimizing interface mismatch will make the mechanical response more consistent with conventional deformation models.
Minor precipitate formation or impurity effects could contribute to the measured mechanical behavior.
